slides.narration: Welcome to Book II, Chapter 4: Understanding Copy Semantics. This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. Modern C++ is not about using the newest syntax because it looks impressive. It is about encoding ownership, lifetime, invariants, generic behavior, and failure boundaries so the program is easier to reason about and harder to misuse.

Push for three layers: the intent, the mechanism, and the evidence. In modern C++, the evidence might be a destructor running, a copy becoming independent, a move leaving ownership in exactly one place, a constrained template rejecting a bad call, or an algorithm producing a predictable sequence.

slides.title: 4.1.2 Using Copy Assignment

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 4, treat 4.1.2 Using Copy Assignment as a design decision with costs and evidence. Copy assignment must consider both the incoming value and the destination’s existing allocation. Deleting the destination first and then attempting allocation can lose the old value if the allocation fails. It can also break self-assignment when source and destination are the same object. The example constructs a temporary copy first. Only after that succeeds does it swap size and storage with the destination. The temporary then destroys the old destination storage. This gives a clear commit point and naturally handles self-assignment, at the cost of allocating a replacement even when existing capacity could potentially be reused. slides.title: 4.2 Distinguishing Shallow and Deep Copies
keyPoints: “Shallow” and “deep” describe which relationships are duplicated, not a universal ranking of good and bad.
Copying a non-owning pointer is a useful shallow observation.
Copying an exclusively owning raw pointer as though it created another independent owner is usually a defect.
A deep copy should follow the intended value boundary, which may be more complicated than recursively copying.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 4, treat 4.2.2 Implementing Independent Ownership as a design decision with costs and evidence. The buffer uses std::unique_ptr<int[]> internally to ensure each allocation has one release owner. The explicit copy constructor allocates a fresh owned array, so exclusivity remains true while value copying becomes possible at the enclosing type level. The invariant couples size_ and data_: a positive size must correspond to storage for that many integers; a zero-sized buffer uses an empty pointer. swap exchanges both parts together and is nonthrowing for this representation. Exchanging only one member would violate the invariant even though each individual member remained a valid C++ object. slides.title: Walk through the state transition
keyPoints: Before assignment, the destination might contain one integer while the source contains three.
The algorithm first constructs a three-element candidate.
At that stage there are three independent buffer objects: source, old destination, and candidate.
The source never changes.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 4, treat Walk through the state transition as a design decision with costs and evidence. Before assignment, the destination might contain one integer while the source contains three. The algorithm first constructs a three-element candidate. At that stage there are three independent buffer objects: source, old destination, and candidate. The source never changes. If candidate construction fails, its completed resources are cleaned up and the old destination remains accepted. At the swap, the destination takes the candidate’s representation. The temporary takes the old destination’s representation. No element-by-element modification of the accepted destination is required after commit. Finally the temporary is destroyed, releasing the previous destination. Draw sizes next to storage owners at every step; this catches an incomplete swap immediately. slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 4, treat Evidence and interpretation as a design decision with costs and evidence. The original first element remains seven while the copy becomes 99. Assignment changes the destination’s size from one to three and copies the source value. Self-assignment leaves it valid, and assigning the empty buffer produces size zero with checked access failing. Trace assignment as three states: construct the candidate, swap the candidate with the destination, destroy the former destination now held by the temporary. Before the swap, failure leaves the destination unchanged. After the swap, cleanup is handled by the temporary’s owning member. The integer-element model keeps the copy loop itself nonthrowing. slides.title: Failure clinic — Delete, then allocate
keyPoints: The naïve assignment first frees the destination’s old allocation, then allocates replacement storage.
If the second step fails, the old value has already been destroyed.
A catch block cannot recreate it without some other saved copy.
Setting the pointer to null avoids a double release but does not restore the promised value.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 4, treat Failure clinic — Delete, then allocate as a design decision with costs and evidence. The naïve assignment first frees the destination’s old allocation, then allocates replacement storage. If the second step fails, the old value has already been destroyed. A catch block cannot recreate it without some other saved copy. Setting the pointer to null avoids a double release but does not restore the promised value. This implementation may support a weaker documented guarantee, but it cannot honestly claim preservation of the previous accepted buffer. A different defect swaps only the pointer. Tests that inspect only the first element may still pass because both old and new allocations have an element at index zero. A size query or boundary access exposes the inconsistency. This is why the supplied tests assign differently sized values, include an empty source, and examine checked access afterward. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 4, treat Review answers and solution notes as a design decision with costs and evidence. Copy-and-swap preserves the destination until a complete candidate exists. It also handles self-assignment without a special branch, although it may perform unnecessary allocation in that case. Swapping every coupled member preserves the size/storage invariant. A vector member already provides suitable value and resource semantics for this application, so the enclosing class can often follow the Rule of Zero. Begin with a destination containing two distinct values and a source containing three. Inject failure while constructing the candidate’s second element. Verify destination size, every destination value, source size, and every source value after rejection. Then disable the injected failure and repeat the assignment successfully. Extend the test to failure on the first and last copied elements. Include an empty source and self-assignment. Reset the injection policy explicitly between cases so one case cannot silently change the next case’s starting conditions. Compare semantic values rather than allocator addresses; an allocator is allowed to reuse released addresses.
